name: LDO vs Buck Advisor
blurb: efficiency, heat and noise of an LDO against a buck, side by side
intro: An LDO burns the whole voltage drop as heat but is quiet and simple; a buck is efficient but switches. This puts both (and a buck followed by an LDO) side by side for your rail: input current, efficiency, dissipation, junction temperature and output noise, and says which fits.

inputs.label: Buck efficiency at this load
inputs.help: From the buck's datasheet curve at your Vin, Vout and load.

inputs.label: Load is noise-sensitive (ADC reference, RF, audio, PLL)

examples.title: 5 V USB to 3.3 V at 300 mA
12 V to 3.3 V at 500 mA for a radio

usage: Give input and output voltage (V), load current (A, 300m accepted), ambient °C, the LDO package (sets θJA), LDO dropout in mV and quiescent current in µA, the buck's efficiency in % at this load from its datasheet, the buck's output ripple in mV p-p, and quiet=true if the load is noise-sensitive. It returns efficiency, input current, dissipation and junction temperature for an LDO, a buck and a buck followed by an LDO, plus a recommendation with the reason. Use it when choosing the regulator for one rail.
sources: LDO: P = (Vin − Vout)·Iout + Vin·Iq, Tj = Ta + P·θJA (TI SLVA118A, Digital Designer's Guide to Linear Voltage Regulators and Thermal Management)
θJA values: typical JEDEC 2s2p figures from regulator datasheets (rule of thumb)
Buck light-load curve: full-load loss scaled as 2 % fixed + 68 % linear + 30 % I² (rule-of-thumb model of an auto-PFM buck)
